name: Deoxyarbutin

lead: Deoxyarbutin is a lab-made relative of arbutin used as a topical lightener to fade age spots, melasma and other dark patches and even out skin tone.

It competes with tyrosine at tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, so less pigment forms; studies describe the inhibition as reversible. A 2005 paper reported skin lightening in a pigmented guinea pig model and stronger tyrosinase inhibition than hydroquinone or arbutin in a test-tube assay. Randomized human trials were not found in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is applied as a cream or serum directly to the dark areas, typically with daily sunscreen, since sun exposure re-darkens pigment. Lightening products of this kind are used over weeks to months.
Researchers have compared its safety with hydroquinone in cultured cells and examined the cytotoxicity of UVB-irradiated forms. Regulatory status was not established in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Applied to fade age spots, melasma and dark patches for a more even tone. It blocks tyrosinase, so less melanin forms. Evidence comes mostly from lab and animal work.

lead: Deoxyarbutin (dA) is a synthetic derivative of arbutin that inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and has been developed as a topical skin-lightening agent for hyperpigmentation such as age spots and melasma [1][2].

It was described in a 2005 paper as a reversible tyrosinase inhibitor with skin-lightening activity in a pigmented guinea pig model and with inhibition of mushroom tyrosinase more potent than hydroquinone or arbutin in vitro [1]. Later laboratory work has examined its safety relative to hydroquinone, and its stability in formulations [3][4]. The sources reviewed contain no randomized human trial results for deoxyarbutin as a cosmetic.

paras: Tyrosinase inhibitors of this type resemble the enzyme's substrate, tyrosine, and compete for the catalytic site; deoxyarbutin was designed on this premise [1]. A 2008 study reported on the mechanism of inhibition by deoxyarbutin and its second-generation derivatives [2]. Another study found that deoxyarbutin and derivatives reduced tyrosinase activity and melanin synthesis without inducing reactive oxygen species or apoptosis in the cells tested [5].

A 2022 comparison of tyrosinase inhibitors noted that reported results for kojic acid, arbutins and deoxyarbutin differ between articles, and examined these compounds against mushroom tyrosinase and cultured B16F10 cells [6].

The safety of hydroquinone and its derivatives as whitening agents has been described as controversial, and a 2009 study compared hydroquinone, arbutin and deoxyarbutin in cultured melanocytes with and without UVA-induced oxidative stress to assess whether deoxyarbutin could be an alternative [3]. A 2017 study examined hydroquinone-mediated cytotoxicity and hypopigmentation effects from UVB-irradiated arbutin and deoxyarbutin [7]. Stability of deoxyarbutin in an anhydrous emulsion has also been studied [4]. A 2006 paper reported a comparative efficacy and safety evaluation [8].

A 2022 animal study investigated deoxyarbutin in severe acute pancreatitis, unrelated to appearance [9]. A 2020 article discusses deoxyarbutin as a hydroquinone alternative for topical skin lightening [10].
No studies found of randomized human trials in the sources reviewed; the evidence consists of in vitro work, an animal (guinea pig) study, and formulation and safety studies [1][3][8].
